items.description_text: Climate change, environmental degradation, and unsustainable consumption patterns are among the most pressing challenges of our time. Young people play a crucial role in driving sustainable change, yet many lack strong motivation to adopt and promote environmentally responsible behaviours. A global citizen is a person who has a global perspective and mindset, understands the global implications of their actions, takes the responsibility attached to them and is constantly making changes in their lives in order to accommodate their impact on the world in a positive manner. Public spaces have a huge potential in terms of informing, raising awareness and fostering global citizenship competencies among community members. Street campaigning is an innovative methodology in youth work and is the key methodology tackled by this particular training course. Street Campaigning differs from “traditional” workshops and other indoor activities, and it is very flexible and adaptable to different contexts and topics. This training will offer the opportunity to different youth workers to explore deeper sustainability topics, responsible global citizenship and develop practical competencies in working with street campaigning. items.description_text: Discover the potential of Youth Exchanges In 3 training days, we show you the possibilities Erasmus+ Youth Exchanges have to offer for young people from disadvantaged backgrounds. An international youth project might just be the life-changing opportunity for the disadvantaged young people you are working with: e.g. those from minority backgrounds, with special needs, with socio-economic difficulties, discriminated groups, in difficult situations, with limited opportunities... Why participate? International Youth Exchanges are a rewarding methodology to reach your organisation’s inclusion aims. This Youth Exchanges for ALL course gives you concrete examples of what is possible, brings you in contact with other inclusion youth organisations (from Europe and EuroMed), shows you what funding is available specifically for youth inclusion projects and walks you step-by-step through the process in case you would like to give it a try. This course is for NEWCOMERS to Erasmus+ Youth (e.g. youth worker, social worker,...) who are directly working with young people from disadvantaged backgrounds (e.g. facing social, economic, educational, geographic, cultural, health & disability challenges). If you NEVER organised an international youth project with your target group before and would like to know what is possible, then this course is for you! items.description_text: GreenSport 2030 is a European cooperation project under the Erasmus+ Sport programme that supports grassroots sport organisations in transitioning towards more sustainable, digitally enabled, and inclusive practices. The project introduces the GreenSport Hub, an AI-powered platform that allows sport organisations to monitor environmental impact, including energy use, waste, and carbon footprint, and to improve their performance through data-driven insights. In parallel, the project delivers capacity-building activities for youth oriented professions and promotes circular economy solutions such as equipment reuse, and facilitates policy dialogue to integrate sustainability criteria into sport governance and funding mechanisms. Many young people face challenges such as social isolation, stress, anxiety, identity-related difficulties or the long-term effects of exclusion and discrimination. Traditional educational approaches do not always provide the tools or spaces needed to address these experiences. This project explores how movement, theatre and other embodied practices can create more welcoming, engaging and emotionally safe environments where young people can express themselves, build confidence and connect with others. Throughout the training course, participants will explore psychoeducational approaches and practical methods that support psychosocial and emotional development. Through experiential activities, reflection and peer learning, youth workers will develop new tools to help young people strengthen resilience, improve communication, build empathy and manage everyday challenges. Re:Body also responds to the growing challenge of digital overwhelm. By using embodied and offline learning methods, the project encourages participants to reconnect with physical expression, creativity and human interaction as a valuable complement to technology-based learning environments. Beyond the training activities themselves, the project aims to strengthen connections between youth workers across Europe. items.description_text: Unleashing Creativity: From Lens to Life is an Erasmus+ KA153 Training Course for youth workers, facilitators, trainers and educators who are active in the field of youth work and non-formal learning. The training explores how photography and creative methods can be used as practical tools in youth work. The project focuses on two main aspects: using photography to improve the visibility and communication of youth work, using participatory photography to help young people express their experiences, ideas and perspectives. Throughout the training, participants will take part in practical and non-formal learning activities covering photography basics, composition, visual storytelling, creativity methods, Photovoice, the Six Thinking Hats method, digital communication, media literacy and ethical photography. Participants will also explore how photography can support youth participation, advocacy and self-expression, particularly for young people who may find verbal communication difficult. The programme connects these methods with the European Youth Goals, the ETS Competence Model for Youth Workers, YOCOMO and Youthpass. The training is strongly based on learning by doing. Participants will experience the full process themselves: developing ideas, taking photographs, reflecting on their meaning, selecting and editing images, creating visual narratives and preparing their work for presentation. A central part of the programme will be Photovoice, a participatory photography method that allows young people to document issues that are important to them and use images as a starting point for dialogue and participation. During the mobility, participants will experience the complete Photovoice process so that they can later apply the method in their own youth work. items.description_text: We invite youth workers from Programme countries and Southern Mediterranean countries to take part in an international Partnership Building Activity (PBA) in Northern Portugal focused on inclusive youth work with young women, particularly those living in rural, remote or peripheral communities. Young women living in rural and peripheral areas experience unique realities that present both opportunities and challenges. Rural communities often offer strong social connections, a sense of belonging and growing spaces for community engagement, local leadership and social innovation. At the same time, young women may face barriers such as geographical isolation, limited mobility, reduced access to information, fewer educational and professional opportunities, persistent gender stereotypes and less direct access to youth services and international experiences. These factors can particularly affect young women with fewer opportunities, influencing their participation in community life and their awareness of, and access to, local, national and European opportunities. Youth work has an important role to play in recognising the strengths of rural communities while addressing the barriers that prevent young women from fully participating, accessing information and benefiting from the opportunities available to them. Youth workers and youth organisations play an important role in addressing these inequalities. They can create inclusive spaces, provide information, accompany young women in accessing opportunities and develop practices that respond to the realities of their communities. The PBA will bring together youth workers from E+ and ESC Programme and Southern Mediterranean countries to exchange experiences and reflect on how their organisations engage young women, remove barriers and make opportunities more visible, accessible and inclusive. Today, young people face a significant increase in anxiety, stress, and isolation. Traditional, talk-based youth work methods often have limitations when it comes to facilitating deep emotional expression. This project responds directly to the lack of practical, creative tools available to youth workers by introducing art as a medium for healing and communication. The 9-day training will take place in Antalya, Türkiye, from October 18 to 26, 2026. Project Objectives By blending non-formal education with creative expression, the project aims to: Equip youth workers with a new toolkit of art-based, non-verbal methods. Develop skills in creating psychologically safe spaces using a trauma-informed approach. Enhance competence in facilitating sensitive emotional processes. Promote self-care and resilience as professional practices to prevent youth worker burnout. Enable youth workers to take on more active roles in supporting the well-being of the most vulnerable youth. Provide equal opportunities for expression for young people who face communication barriers or social exclusion due to anxiety. We are looking for 32 participants (youth workers and young people) from Finland, Türkiye, Romania, Poland, and Italy. items.description_text: What is The Edge Effect? In ecology, the edge effect describes the place where two different ecosystems meet. These transition zones are often the richest and most diverse environments, where new relationships emerge and life flourishes. We believe learning works in much the same way. Growth often happens at the edges—where different cultures meet, where comfort zones are gently expanded, and where diverse experiences come together to create something new. The Edge Effect is an Erasmus+ Training Course designed for youth workers, educators, facilitators and community leaders who want to explore regenerative approaches to learning, facilitation and community building. Throughout the week, we will explore how nature can inspire educational practice, how communities can become powerful learning environments, and how non-formal education can help young people develop resilience, participation and a stronger connection with themselves, others and the natural world. Rather than focusing only on theories, we will experiment, reflect and learn together through direct experience. Our Objectives By the end of the training, participants will: • Explore regenerative and nature-inspired approaches to facilitation. • Strengthen their confidence in designing meaningful learning experiences. • Develop practical tools for community building and group facilitation. • Experience non-formal education through immersive, participatory methods. • Discover how reflection supports personal and professional growth. • Exchange practices and ideas with participants from across Europe. • Build lasting international connections for future cooperation. Above all, we hope every participant leaves feeling inspired to bring new ideas, renewed energy and a deeper sense of purpose back to their own community. Who is this Training For? items.description_text: EmpathyLab is an Erasmus+ Training Course taking place in Rimini, Italy, from 19 to 24 October 2026, bringing together 15 youth workers and educators from Italy, Poland and Spain. The activity is specifically addressed to people who are already active in the field of youth work and non-formal learning, particularly those working with young people, vulnerable groups or communities facing social exclusion and fewer opportunities. The training will focus on empathy, inclusion, human rights and anti-discrimination, providing participants with practical methods they can use in their educational and youth work activities. Through non-formal education, participants will explore tools such as group discussions, role-play, simulations, case studies, storytelling and experiential learning. Particular attention will be given to how to create safe spaces for dialogue, manage group dynamics, encourage perspective-taking and support young people in understanding experiences different from their own. Participants will also work with the EmpathyLab Toolkit and reflect on how its methods can be adapted to their own local contexts. The course is designed not only as a learning experience, but also as a multiplier activity. After the international training, participants will be encouraged to apply what they have learned and contribute to the organisation of local EmpathyLab activities or workshops in their communities. We are therefore looking for applicants who are actively involved in youth work or non-formal education, motivated to exchange practices with an international group and willing to transfer the learning into their future work with young people.

items.description_text: Background and Rationale Despite the increasing attention to youth participation in democratic processes and decision-making promoted by Erasmus+ and the European Solidarity Corps, many young people with fewer opportunities - due to social, economic, cultural, geographical, or educational barriers - remain underrepresented and unheard. For example, as indicated by the YPS monitoring (Dr. Dan Moxon, YPS Steering group, 2024), between 2021 and 2023, only 9.8% of participants in Erasmus+ Youth projects with participation themes were young people with fewer opportunities (YPFO) (considerably lower than the 30% of estimated participants in Erasmus+ KA1 activities (Youth Exchanges, Youth Workers Mobility and Youth Participation activities) who are YPFO). Youth workers, educators, and trainers are key actors in supporting these young people, but they often lack practical tools and knowledge to address the specific challenges these youth face when engaging in democratic life. This study visit is part of a long-term project organised by SALTO Inclusion & Diversity and SALTO Participation & Information, which aims to strengthen competences to design and facilitate inclusive, accessible, and meaningful democratic participation processes with diverse groups of young people. What do we mean by democratic participation? items.description_text: Across Europe, democratic values are increasingly under pressure, and public discourse is becoming more polarised. Amid these developments, youth work stands at a crossroads: socially and politically relevant enough to matter yet increasingly expected to remain “apolitical” and focus on individual life skills. Youth work practitioners often find themselves navigating difficult dilemmas, such as how youth work can operate effectively in politically volatile and polarised environments, what its role is in safeguarding democracy, and whether depoliticisation is a viable response or itself a political choice. And if not, how can youth workers navigate the risks and responsibilities of taking a stand for democracy? The seminar targets youth work practitioners who want to strengthen democratic values and attitudes amongst their target group and within their communities, and exchange ideas and experiences with like-minded colleagues. In particular, the seminar aims to offer a space for youth work practitioners to: -explore the current state of democracy and better understand its implications for youth work and young people's lives; -reflect on the ethical and political dimensions of youth work and its role in promoting and sustaining democratic values; -examine existing projects, initiatives, and practices that have responded to democratic backsliding and critically reflect on what worked well and what was less effective; -enable and support participants in finding the right approach in their youth work to strengthen and support democratic values in their local context; -encourage participants to develop concrete follow-up activities for their local youth work and communities. (Guidance and advice will be provided by the seminar facilitators.); -build a supportive network of youth work practitioners committed to democracy, enabling continued exchange, peer support, and cooperation beyond the seminar itself. The training neither aims to inform about nor discuss the details and/or history of any specific war. items.title: PLAY IS HUMAN RIGHT – The neuroscience of joy and the NVC practice of connection
items.summary: Inspired by Jaak Panksepp’s affective neuroscience and Nonviolent Communication (NVC), this webinar explores how the PLAY system supports connection, resilience, creativity, and emotional wellbeing.

items.description_text: In Jaak Panksepp’s affective neuroscience, PLAY is one of the brain’s primary emotional systems—a neural circuit that supports connection, flexibility, learning, resilience, and social trust. And yet, in many adult lives, especially in work, parenting, leadership, and intimate relationships, play often disappears first. During this webinar, we will explore the PLAY circuit through the lens of Nonviolent Communication (NVC). Together, we will discover why play requires a sense of safety, how joy differs from entertainment or performance, and how a playful presence can soften tension, open space for dialogue, and support our needs for connection, freedom, creativity, ease, and belonging. We will also ask: What happens to our relationships when play is absent? Why do we sometimes lose access to lightness, curiosity, and spontaneity? How can sharing NVC help us bring play back without forcing it, bypassing pain, or pretending everything is okay? Where playfulness can support sharing and learning NVC? This webinar is for people who want to understand play not as a luxury, but as a deep human need and a powerful doorway to empathy, regulation, and more alive relationships. It is a result of the Erasmus + training course “Flying Giraffes” that took place in Poland in June 2026. items.description_text: Do you sometimes feel overwhelmed by your emotions and wish you could understand them better? Would you like to respond to difficult situations with more awareness, empathy, and choice? Emotions are not something to fix, hide, or “manage away.” They are signals that tell us what matters, what hurts, what we long for, and what may need our attention. In this webinar, we will explore emotions through the lens of Nonviolent Communication (NVC). We will look at how to recognise and name feelings, listen to the needs beneath them, stay present when emotions become intense, and move from automatic reaction towards greater connection and conscious choice. items.description_text: Creative Circles: Voices is an exploratory training course for youth workers, educators, mentors, facilitators and trainers working in the field of non-formal learning and youth work. The training explores voice as a tool for self-expression, connection and participation. Through music, singing, rhythm, improvisation, storytelling and embodied practices, participants will explore their relationship with their own voice, what they want to express, what may be difficult to express, and what happens when different voices meet. The learning journey moves from the individual towards the collective through three main focuses: Finding My Voice, Expressing My Voice and Voices Together. Participants will work with body, breath, resonance, movement, sound and silence, as well as collective singing, storytelling and improvisation. We will also explore questions of participation: who gets heard, who remains silent, and how youth workers can create spaces where young people feel able to find and use their own voices. The training is based on experiential and non-formal learning. Participants will learn by doing, experimenting, reflecting and creating together rather than learning how to sing or perform. A significant part of the programme will take place outdoors, using nature as an active element of the learning process. Throughout the week, visiting practitioners will introduce different approaches to voice, music and storytelling. Together, participants will also collect and document methods and exercises that can be adapted and used in their own youth work practice. No previous musical, singing or storytelling experience is required. The training is intended for people actively involved in youth work and non-formal learning who are curious about using creative and embodied approaches in their work with young people.

items.description_text: Wellness Navigators Webinar Series Wellness Navigators is a series of six free online webinars created for youth workers, educators, trainers, facilitators, and anyone interested in supporting the emotional and social well-being of young people. Running from September 2026 to February 2027, the series explores practical approaches to well-being through the four dimensions of the Wellness Compass: Body, Mind, Emotions, and Connection. Each webinar combines accessible theory with practical tools, reflection, and experiential activities that can be used both for personal development and in educational work with young people. Topics include emotional awareness and regulation, connection and empathy, body-based practices, play and joy, and everyday strategies for strengthening resilience and well-being. The webinars are part of the Wellness Navigators Erasmus+ project, which develops practical educational resources to help young people better recognise their needs, understand their emotional and bodily signals, build healthier relationships, and navigate everyday challenges with greater awareness and choice. What to expect Participants will: discover practical tools for supporting youth well-being; explore the connection between body, thoughts, emotions, and relationships; learn experiential activities that can be adapted to youth work and non-formal education; gain inspiration from approaches such as Nonviolent Communication, embodiment, mindfulness, creative methods, and emotional education; receive access to webinar recordings and additional project resources. The webinars are free of charge and open to an international audience. Participants can register once for the whole six-part series and receive information and access links before each session. The Council of Europe and European Commission highlight that young people are currently experiencing and will continue to bear the brunt of worsening climate impacts, making climate action not only an environmental issue but a matter of intergenerational justice. Youth engagement is increasingly recognised as a decisive force in achieving Europe’s green transition. Both formal (school systems, civic participation structures) and informal (community projects, youth work) pathways empower young people to contribute to environmental action. The European Green Deal support initiatives emphasise that youth bring creativity, fresh perspectives, and a direct stake in long‑term climate solutions, making their involvement indispensable. The Council of Europe’s groundbreaking Recommendation on Young People and Climate Action stresses that young people must be meaningfully included in climate decision‑making processes. The recommendation highlights the need to protect young climate defenders, ensure access to rights, and remove structural barriers preventing youth from influencing policy. We are living through times of ecological, social, and political crisis. Geopolitical tensions, deep societal divisions, and environmental changes have created a heavy, exhausting sense of uncertainty. Entrepreneurial Resilience Through Improv.“ This project is designed for youth workers, trainers, facilitators, educators, and anyone working with young people who want to explore entrepreneurship in a more practical, creative, and human way. For us, entrepreneurship is not about business creation or financial models. It is a mindset. items.description_text: This international training activity aims to introduce and promote a Self-Assessment Tool for Quality Work with Young People developed in Malta, while strengthening the capacity of youth organisations to embed quality assurance into their everyday practice. Through interactive workshops, peer learning, and practical exercises, participants will develop skills in reflective practice, evaluation, and participatory quality assurance processes. The activity is designed for youth workers, organisation leaders, NGO managers, board members, and representatives of National Agencies and umbrella bodies who support quality development in the youth sector. It will provide a space to exchange tools, approaches, and evidence-based strategies from different countries, fostering organisational learning, accountability, and continuous improvement. By the end of the training, participants will have increased their capacity to assess and enhance the quality of their work, gained practical experience in using quality assurance tools applicable within the Erasmus+ Youth Programme and beyond, developed draft organisational action plans and evidence portfolios, and established new partnerships that could lead to future KA2 cooperation projects focused on organisational development. Logistics & Accommodation The activity will take place from 23–27 November 2026 in Malta. Participants will be accommodated at Paradise Bay Hotel in Mellieħa, with accommodation and meals provided throughout the activity. 23 November: Arrival of participants and welcome dinner 24–26 November: Training activity days 27 November: Departure of participants The above is a draft schedule and may be adjusted slightly as the programme is developed.

items.description_text: A waiting room. A youth centre. A public square. A restroom. A courtroom. Most spaces used by young people are designed by adults. Adults decide what is needed, what feels safe and what feels welcoming. But how often do we ask young people what they think? And more importantly, how often do we invite them to create these spaces with us? The idea for this training comes from a cocreation project in which four unaccompanied minors worked with judges, guardians and children's rights experts to redesign a courtroom for the Belgian Council for Alien Law Litigation. Their ideas helped create a space that felt calmer, clearer and more respectful. The project showed that when young people are treated as equal partners, everyone benefits, including the adults who use and work in these spaces. Why does this matter? The spaces young people use every day influence how they feel, act and connect with others. When they help shape these spaces, they build confidence, ownership and a stronger sense of belonging. At the same time, the whole community can benefit from spaces that better reflect the needs and experiences of the people who use them. This training explores how youth workers can set up cocreation processes that enable young people to actively shape the spaces around them. Moving beyond participation, we focus on working together, sharing responsibility and creating solutions that reflect young people's experiences and needs. (young people: pre-teenagers, teenagers, young adults) What to expect? items.description_text: Storybuilders Lab: From Story to STEAM Challenge in Youth Work is a practice-based e-learning course for youth workers, youth leaders, trainers and facilitators who want to explore how storytelling, creative construction and STEAM can become tools for participation, problem solving and non-formal learning. Many STEAM activities start with a predefined outcome: build a bridge, create a vehicle, follow these instructions. Storybuilders Lab explores a different approach. The facilitator defines the learning intention, but participants influence the story, identify the problem and decide what needs to be created. The methodology follows a simple learning cycle: STORY → QUESTION → IDEAS → CHALLENGE → DESIGN → MAKE → TEST → IMPROVE → REFLECT → STORY CONTINUES Participants will learn how to use story triggers, mystery objects and open questions to generate curiosity and meaningful challenges. They will explore Story Democracy, a participatory method for collecting, combining and developing different ideas so that the direction of a project is not predetermined by the facilitator or dominated by the strongest voices in the group. A central part of the course is hands-on prototyping. Participants will work with accessible materials such as cardboard, recyclable materials and simple construction tools to turn ideas into physical prototypes. Makedo or similar cardboard-construction tools may be used where available, but no specialised equipment is required. The focus is not on creating a perfect final object. Participants practise an iterative process of: Make → Test → Notice → Change → Test again This allows them to explore how experimentation, “failure”, debugging and redesign can become valuable learning experiences in youth work. The course also addresses inclusive participation. items.description_text: Das Training richtet sich an Fachkräfte der Jugendarbeit sowie an Entscheidungsträgerinnen und Entscheidungsträger, die sich mit der Gestaltung, Entwicklung und politischen Rahmung von Räumen für junge Menschen befassen. Ziel des Trainings ist es, neue Perspektiven auf jugendgerechte Orte zu eröffnen und innovative Modelle kennenzulernen, die Begegnung, Austausch und selbstbestimmte Nutzung ermöglichen. Ausgangspunkt bildet der in Luxemburg formulierte Bedarf junger Menschen nach frei zugänglichen, sicheren und attraktiven Orten, an denen sie sich treffen, Zeit miteinander verbringen, Erlebnisse teilen und Erfahrungen sammeln können. Das Training greift diesen Bedarf auf und lädt dazu ein, das Angebot an Räumen für Jugendliche neu zu denken und weiterzuentwickeln. Im Rahmen des Trainings werden europäische Praxisbeispiele aus Belgien, Südtirol, der Schweiz und Deutschland vorgestellt. Sie zeigen, wie Räume für junge Menschen in unterschiedlichen Kontexten gestaltet und betrieben werden können. Ergänzend werden die luxemburgischen Rahmenbedingungen beleuchtet. Die Teilnehmenden haben die Möglichkeit, sich mit Vertreterinnen und Vertretern der vorgestellten Organisationen auszutauschen und Einblicke in deren Arbeitsweisen, Herausforderungen und Erfolgsfaktoren zu gewinnen. Ein weiterer Programmpunkt ist die Besichtigung eines vom nationalen Jugenddienst geführten Maker Space. Die Teilnehmenden lernen vor Ort ein konkretes Praxisbeispiel kennen und können sich mit den verantwortlichen Fachkräften austauschen. Das Training bietet Raum für Reflexion, Diskussion und Vernetzung. Es unterstützt die Teilnehmenden dabei, neue Ansätze kennenzulernen und Anregungen für die eigene Praxis mitzunehmen. Ziel ist es, Impulse für die Weiterentwicklung jugendgerechter Räume in Europa zu setzen und Angebote nachhaltig an den Bedürfnissen junger Menschen auszurichten.

Across Europe, youth workers increasingly encounter young people experiencing stress, anxiety, loneliness, burnout, and other mental health challenges. While youth workers are often a trusted source of support, many feel they lack practical tools and confidence to respond effectively. MindBoost Academy has been designed to strengthen their competences through experiential learning, international cooperation, and the exchange of good practices. A central outcome of the training is the co-creation of the MindBoost Toolkit—a practical collection of methods, activities, facilitation guides, and resources that participants will design together throughout the week. Rather than simply testing existing materials, participants will actively contribute their own experiences, ideas, and expertise to develop tools that can be adapted and implemented in youth work settings across different communities. During six days in Breda, participants will: - strengthen their understanding of youth mental health and wellbeing; - explore practical, non-formal education methods for promoting resilience and emotional wellbeing; - develop facilitation, mentoring, and peer-support skills; - learn how to recognise challenges and respond appropriately within the role of a youth worker; - co-create the MindBoost Toolkit, ensuring it reflects diverse experiences and practical needs from both partner countries; - build lasting connections with fellow youth workers and organisations. items.description_text: Are you a youth leader or youth worker committed to becoming an agent of change in your local community and beyond? Are you interested in learning more about what quality youth participation means and how you can embed it in your organisational life or the new projects that you plan? Do you want to explore the opportunities of the Erasmus+ Programme? Then “Dive into Youth Participation” is the Training Course for you! Youth participation in democratic life and young people's active civic engagement are high priorities of the EU Youth Strategy and are incorporated into the majority of contemporary youth policy frameworks in different European countries. The Erasmus+ Programme is one of the mechanisms to put the EU Youth Strategy into practice and provide many opportunities for young people to develop international projects, which empower them to take an active role in society and help them develop civic and social competencies. In this context, the fourth edition of the Training Course “Dive into Youth Participation” brings together 25 youth leaders and youth workers from different European countries with an aim to improve their understanding and practices toward quality youth participation. This is also an opportunity to learn more about the possibilities within the Erasmus+ Key Action 154 “Youth Participation Activities” and how to ensure youth participation is properly implemented in all stages of a project or participation initiative. items.description_text: Why this programme? Young people increasingly experience the world through digital, visual, interactive and participatory media. At the same time, heritage education can sometimes remain centred on traditional formats: guided tours, exhibitions, historical information and passive observation. This creates an opportunity for youth work. New media can provide alternative entry points into heritage, allowing young people to: explore places and stories through immersive experiences; discover hidden or forgotten narratives; connect personal and community memories with wider European heritage; question dominant interpretations of history; create their own narratives; collaborate across cultures; transform physical spaces into interactive learning environments. The programme therefore does not aim to turn youth trainers into technology specialists. Instead, it aims to help them become creative facilitators who know when, why and how to use technology to create meaningful learning experiences. General aim To strengthen the capacity of youth trainers to use new media and emerging technologies as tools for heritage awareness, intercultural learning, creativity and youth participation. Specific objectives By the end of the training, participants will be able to: Explore contemporary approaches to cultural heritage and heritage awareness. Identify opportunities for using immersive and interactive media in youth work. Experiment with VR, AR, 360° media, projection mapping, interactive installations, digital storytelling and other creative technologies. Design non-formal education activities connecting young people with local, national and European heritage. Use storytelling and participatory methodologies to make heritage more relevant to young people. Encourage young people to question, reinterpret and remix heritage narratives. items.description_text: The project arises from a shared observation among young people, community development professionals, and partner organizations: a growing need to reconnect with the living world, rebuild social bonds, and collectively reflect on current ecological challenges in the face of the climate emergency. It addresses two main needs: Strengthening the skills of facilitators and community leaders so they can design and implement educational projects with strong social and ecological impact. Actively engaging young people in meaningful, concrete, and transformative projects. The project uses the living garden as an educational, sensory, and cooperative tool, helping to recreate connections between humans and ecosystems. These spaces become platforms for social transformation, civic education, and territorial resilience. It is based on active pedagogy that promotes autonomy, local engagement, and the transversal skills required for the ecological transition.
